JSON: Name: tba_ehps_pipeline Title: Dual-heterogeneous-noise adversarial pipeline for compromising expressive human pose and shape estimation models Short Hypothesis: Adversarial perturbations produced by a dual heterogeneous noise generator combining a VAE-based image perturbation and a ControlNet-guided conditioned perturbation, optimized with a multi-gradient adversarial loss and iterative PGD, will cause larger increases in EHPS estimation error (MPJPE/MPVPE) than perturbations from single-source generators or standard gradient attacks under the same L_infty perturbation budget. Related Work: Existing EHPS research prioritizes accuracy of body, hand and face parameter recovery using parametric models (e.g., SMPL-X variants, foundation models) and transformer or CNN backbones, with limited attention to adversarial robustness. Prior adversarial work has focused on image classification and object detection defenses and on skeleton-based action recognition attacks; a smaller body of work targets pose estimation networks using per-pixel gradient attacks, selective pixel perturbation, or temporal-coherent skeleton perturbations. These prior methods either (1) generate perturbations for classification/detection objectives rather than full parametric EHPS outputs, (2) perturb sparse joint locations without directly maximizing deviations in dense SMPL-like parameter spaces (pose, shape, expression), (3) rely on single-mode noise generation that limits diversity and control, or (4) trade off imperceptibility and effectiveness without a joint noise-model optimization. No existing approach combines learned heterogeneous noise generators with conditioning modules and multi-gradient optimization against EHPS foundation models to improve transferability and controllability. Abstract: This research pipeline defines a targeted adversarial framework for evaluating and exposing robustness weaknesses in expressive human pose and shape estimation (EHPS) models. The proposed pipeline integrates a Dual Heterogeneous Noise Generator—a variational autoencoder producing image-space perturbations and a ControlNet-conditioned generator producing spatially controlled perturbations—into a multi-gradient optimization loop. An adversarial loss that directly measures deviations in EHPS outputs (pose, shape, expression) is combined with pixel-level consistency constraints; iterative PGD refinement uses gradients from both the noise generator and the target EHPS model to maximize parameter deviations under an L_infty bound. The pipeline is designed to generate transferable, controllable adversarial samples for black-box and white-box evaluations across SMPL-X family models and other EHPS systems. The primary contribution is a reproducible experimental protocol and ablation suite that quantifies how heterogeneous noise sources and multi-gradient optimization affect attack potency, transferability, and perceptual visibility, enabling rigorous assessment of EHPS security and informing future defenses. Experiments: Datasets: 3DPW (in-the-wild RGB + SMPL annotations) and UBody (whole-body, hand, face labels); use held-out test splits not used for any generator fine-tuning. Models (targets): SMPLer-X family (S,B,L,H), Hand4Whole, OSX. Baselines: (A) FGSM (L_infty), (B) PGD (standard), (C) VAE-only noise generator with same adversarial loss, (D) ControlNet-only noise generator, (E) random Gaussian/patch perturbations. Proposed method: DHNG (VAE+ControlNet) + adversarial loss + PGD refinement (TBA). Metrics: MPJPE, PA-MPJPE, MPVPE, PA-MPVPE, percent error growth over clean, L_infty and L_2 norms of perturbations, LPIPS and SSIM for perceptual visibility, transferability measured as relative error increase on held-out models, and human perceptibility MOS using n>=30 raters on randomized image subsets. Experimental setup: single NVIDIA A100 or equivalent, batch size 8, epsilon (L_infty)=8/255 and 16/255; PGD steps: 40 (white-box) and 20 (black-box refinement); learning rates and optimizer seeds fixed; run each attack on 1000 test images per dataset; report mean and 95% confidence intervals. Evaluation protocol: (1) White-box: craft adversarial examples with gradients of each target model and evaluate self-model degradation. (2) Black-box transfer: craft using SMPLer-X-H and evaluate all other targets. (3) Ablations: remove VAE (ControlNet-only), remove ControlNet (VAE-only), remove adversarial loss (optimize only perceptual loss), replace multi-gradient update with single-source gradient, and vary textual conditioning for ControlNet with at least 4 prompt variants; report metric deltas per ablation. Statistical tests: paired t-test between proposed method and top baseline for MPJPE at p<0.01. Deliverables: per-model tables, CDFs of joint error shifts, visual examples, and MOS results. Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Perceptibility: generated adversarial examples may produce visible artifacts (color shifts, local blur) reducing stealth and practical applicability. 2) Transferability limits: attacks optimized on one foundation model may not transfer uniformly to architectures with different inductive biases or training data, limiting generalization. 3) Dataset bias: conclusions drawn from 3DPW and UBody may not generalize to other capture conditions (extreme occlusion, low-light, heavy clothing). 4) Evaluation bounds: L_infty budget choices strongly affect perceived potency; results are sensitive to epsilon selection. 5) Compute and reproducibility: multi-component optimization (VAE, ControlNet, PGD) requires significant GPU resources, potentially limiting replication. 6) Defense arms race: demonstrated vulnerabilities may prompt defenses that invalidate assumptions of transferability, reducing long-term reproducibility of attack rankings. 7) Ethical and misuse risk: methods can be repurposed for malicious manipulation of avatars or privacy-invasive attacks; research outputs must be shared with responsible-use restrictions. 8) Metric limitations: MPJPE/MPVPE capture geometric deviation but do not fully quantify semantic or downstream behavioral impacts of corrupted EHPS outputs.
